Connect a HiLink or traditional 4G/LTE USB modem to UAVcast-Pro, with automatic APN detection, SIM PIN, auto-reconnect and modem signal information for flying over cellular. A 4G/LTE modem gives the drone internet access wherever there's cellular coverage, so telemetry and video reach your ground station far beyond Wi-Fi range. UAVcast-Pro supports HiLink modems, which connect by themselves, and Traditional (PPP) modems, which UAVcast-Pro connects through ModemManager. For traditional modems it finds the APN automatically, connects at boot and reconnects after drops. Open Modem in the sidebar. <drone-ip>/modem Modem page with Traditional (PPP) selected and the APN left on Automatic, before a modem is plugged in.
k: UAVcast-Pro, UAVmatrix, Fleet Manager, drone 4G LTE, MAVLink, ArduPilot, PX4, QGroundControl, Mission Planner, Raspberry Pi drone video

c: HiLinkTraditional (PPP) How it appears A network card (usb0 or eth1). The modem runs its own router and web page, often at 192.168.8.1. A modem device managed by ModemManager. The connection usually appears as ppp0 or wwan0. Who connects The modem itself. UAVcast-Pro, through ModemManager and NetworkManager. Settings in UAVcast-Pro None. Set the APN in the modem's own web page if needed. APN (optional), username, password, PIN. Examples Huawei E3372h, E8372 Huawei E3372s, Quectel EC25 / EG25, Sierra Wireless Not sure? Plug it in and run mmcli -L on the drone. If ModemManager lists it, use Traditional (PPP). If not, and a new network interface appears in Networks, it's HiLink.

Insert a data SIM and plug the modem into the companion computer. Go to Modem. Set Enable modem to Yes and Modem type to Traditional (PPP). Leave Access Point Name (Optional) empty. UAVcast-Pro detects it. Enter PIN code (Optional) if your SIM asks for one. Wait 30 to 90 seconds. Modem Information shows the operator, technology and IPv4 Information once connected. A plugged-in modem connects automatically. If you select Disconnect, it stays disconnected until you connect it again, also after a reboot.

With the APN field empty, UAVcast-Pro tries, in this order: the APN that worked last time with this SIM's operator, the network's default (empty APN), the APN the modem attached to LTE with, the operator's internet APNs from the mobile broadband provider database. The first one that gets an internet address is saved for that operator. Put in a new SIM from another operator and it detects again. If your operator needs a special APN (private APN, M2M or corporate SIMs), type it in. A user-set APN is the only one tried.

Plug the modem in. Wait until its LED shows a solid connection. On Modem, set Enable modem to Yes and Modem type to HiLink. Check Hilink Modem Information: you should see the Interface and an IP Address. HiLink modems connect, choose the network and reconnect on their own, so there are no connect buttons. Change the APN, PIN or network mode in the modem's own web page (browse to it from the drone's network, often http://192.168.8.1).

SettingDefaultValuesNotes Enable modem Yes Yes, No Modem type Traditional (PPP) HiLink, Traditional (PPP) Access Point Name (Optional) empty (Automatic) APN from your operator Traditional only. Username (Optional) / Password (Optional) empty Traditional only. Most operators need neither. PIN code (Optional) empty SIM PIN Traditional only. Leave empty if the SIM has no PIN.

For traditional modems, Modem Information shows Signal Quality, Technology (LTE, UMTS …), Unlock Required, State, Manufacturer, IMEI, the network (Operator, Code, Registration), IPv4 Information (IP Address, Gateway, DNS, MTU) and Connection Properties (APN, IP Type, Roaming). The dashboard's Cellular row shows the same signal summary.

On Networks, select Modem Priority (Outdoor Mode) so traffic stays on the modem when Wi-Fi is still in range at take-off. Use a VPN: cellular operators don't give the drone an address your ground station can reach. Turn on the GCS failsafe on the flight controller. Check signal at altitude: coverage is planned for the ground, and the signal changes as you climb.

Connects, then drops under load Usually power. Check the dashboard Power supply row. The Action Logs show each APN attempt and the reason it failed. For more help, see Modem connected but no internet.

Keep a hostname pointed at your drone's changing public IP with UAVcast-Pro Dynamic DNS (No-IP, DynDNS, DuckDNS or a generic URL), and when a VPN is the better choice. Dynamic DNS keeps a hostname, such as mydrone.ddns.net, pointed at the drone's current public IP address. UAVcast-Pro checks the public IP every 5 minutes and updates your DNS provider when it changes. Open Dynamic DNS in the sidebar. Most cellular links need a VPN instead Dynamic DNS only helps if the drone's public IP can receive incoming connections. Most mobile operators put SIM cards behind carrier-grade NAT, so the public IP belongs to the operator, not to your drone. Use a VPN unless your SIM has a public (often "static" or "M2M") IP address. Dynamic DNS doesn't change where UAVcast-Pro sends telemetry and video: those always go to the IP addresses on Ground Control Stations. It's for reaching the drone's web interface or SSH from outside.
k: UAVcast-Pro, UAVmatrix, Fleet Manager, drone 4G LTE, MAVLink, ArduPilot, PX4, QGroundControl, Mission Planner, Raspberry Pi drone video

c: Create a hostname with your DNS provider (No-IP, DynDNS or DuckDNS). In UAVcast-Pro, go to Dynamic DNS. Set Enable Dynamic DNS? to Yes. Choose your DNS System. Enter your account username (the field is labelled Dynamic DNS configuration), your Password and the hostname in Alias. For DuckDNS, put your token in the username field and anything in Password (the form requires it, DuckDNS ignores it). Fields save as you leave them. Select Connect to start the updater. It sends the current IP straight away and then checks every 5 minutes. Disconnect stops it. <drone-ip>/dynamic-dns Dynamic DNS Manager before it is enabled.

Required by the form; ignored for DuckDNS. Alias empty hostname The hostname to update, for example mydrone.ddns.net. Update interval 5 minutes fixed The Dynamic DNS row on the Dashboard shows whether the updater is running. The Action Logs show each update and the provider's reply.

The Networks page shows every network interface on the drone (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, modem, VPN) and which one is the default route. It's also where you choose whether Wi-Fi or the cellular modem is preferred when both are connected. c: When Wi-Fi and the modem are both connected, Linux sends traffic through the one with the lowest route metric. Network Priority sets those metrics for you: OptionUse it whenEffect WiFi Priority (Indoor Mode) On the bench or at home, to save mobile data. Wi-Fi metric 100, modem metric 600. Modem Priority (Outdoor Mode) Before every flight over cellular. Modem metric 100, Wi-Fi metric 600. Auto (System Default) You don't want UAVcast-Pro to change anything. NetworkManager's own metrics. Switch to Modem Priority before take-off If the drone takes off on Wi-Fi priority, the link stays on Wi-Fi until Wi-Fi is lost, then has to fail over to the modem in the air. That causes a gap in telemetry and video. Select Modem Priority (Outdoor Mode) on the ground. The change applies to the active connections without restarting them (Applying changes...). Which connections are changed The Wi-Fi metric is set on the NetworkManager connection named preconfigured, which is the name Raspberry Pi Imager gives the Wi-Fi you enter while flashing. Wi-Fi set up any other way keeps its own metric, and Ethernet is never changed.

The summary cards show Active Interfaces, Default Gateway (and the interface it goes through) and Total Interfaces. Network Interfaces lists each interface with Name, IP Address, Gateway, Status (Active, Inactive, VPN), Speed, Type and which one is Default. Put your drone and ground station on one private network with the Fleet Manager VPN, or your own Tailscale or ZeroTier network, so telemetry and video work over 4G/LTE. Over 4G/LTE your drone gets an address from the mobile operator that your ground station can't reach. A VPN fixes that: the drone and the ground station join the same private network and get fixed addresses on it, wherever they are and whatever network they use. Open Virtual Private Network in the sidebar. The quickest way is the Fleet Manager VPN, which is included with your UAVcast-Pro license. If you already run your own Tailscale tailnet or ZeroTier network, UAVcast-Pro can join that instead. <drone-ip>/private-network Virtual Private Network with Tailscale selected on a drone that is not paired or logged in yet.

Read the UAVcast-Pro dashboard to check the flight controller, GPS, battery, ground station link, cellular, VPN, RTK, video and Raspberry Pi power, temperature and throttling. The dashboard is the pre-flight checklist for the companion computer. One status card tells you whether the flight controller, GPS, battery, ground station link, modem, VPN, RTK, video and power supply are healthy, with a summary such as All systems normal or 2 problems. Below it you find system information, network traffic, memory and storage. Open Dashboard in the sidebar. <drone-ip>/ Dashboard on a bench unit: two problems (no GPS fix, VPN not connected), system information and network traffic.

c: The card has three groups. Each row has a coloured dot: green is fine, amber is a warning, red is a problem. RowExample valuesWhat to do if it's not green Flight controller Armed, Disarmed, Link stopped, Connecting… See Flight controller. GPS 3D fix · 14 satellites, RTK fixed, No fix, No GPS Wait for a fix outdoors, or check the GPS wiring. Battery voltage and percentage Charge or check the flight controller's battery monitor setup. Ground station Sending to 2 · 16 packets/s, Not sending, 1 set up · waiting for flight controller, None set up See Ground control stations. Cellular operator and signal, No modem detected See Cellular modem. VPN Connected, Not connected, Turned off See VPN. RTK corrections Connecting…, Error - check settings, Turned off See NTRIP / RTK. Video Running, Stopped, Turned off See Camera. Dynamic DNS Running, Turned off See Dynamic DNS. Power supply Stable, Voltage too low - use a stronger power supply, Slowed down (heat or power), Voltage dropped since start-up See Power. Service failed - restarting on any row means the service crashed and is being restarted automatically. If it keeps showing, download the logs from Application → Logging.

On a Raspberry Pi, System Information shows Power, CPU throttling and Temperature: Voltage too low - use a stronger power supply: the Pi is under-voltage right now. This causes USB resets, so the modem or flight controller can drop out. Fix the supply before flying. Voltage dropped since start-up: it happened at some point since boot. Often caused by the modem's transmit peaks. Slowed down (heat or power): the CPU is throttled. Video encoding suffers first. Add a heatsink or airflow, or fix the supply. The temperature bar turns red as the Pi approaches its throttling point.

CardShows System Information Operating System, Hardware (CPU and cores), Uptime, power and Temperature. Network Traffic Received and transmitted totals and rates per interface. Choose Last 50 to Last 1000 samples. Handy for checking how much the video uses on the modem. Memory Usage Total, Used and Free. Data is collected every 10 seconds. Storage Total, Used and Free per partition. The charts need a few minutes of data after boot before they show anything.

The first time you open the web interface, a tour offers to walk you through the main pages. You can Skip Tour or choose Never Show Again. Start it again from Application → Settings → Take a Tour. Power problems in detail: Under-voltage and throttling.

Create UAVcast-Pro Data Streams dashboards with charts, gauges and tiles for any MAVLink field or NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT sensor value, with thresholds, history and JSON import/export. Data Streams lets you build your own live telemetry dashboards. Add numeric tiles, line charts, gauges, bars and status lights, and bind each one to any MAVLink value the flight controller sends or any NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT signal from a sensor or injector. Dashboards are stored on the drone, so everyone who opens the web interface sees the same boards. Open Data Streams in the sidebar. Typical uses: a payload operator's screen with sensor readings, an LTE link panel with RSRP and SINR, or a battery and power board for long flights. <drone-ip>/mission-data Data Streams before the first dashboard: Create dashboard starts one.

c: Select Create dashboard (or New dashboard if you already have one), give it a Name and select Create. Select Edit to enter edit mode, then Add widget and pick a type. On the Source tab, search for a signal and pick it. A green dot means samples are arriving. Set the title, units and decimals on Display, limits and colour thresholds on Range, and chart options on Chart. Select Save. Drag and resize widgets, then select Done. Only admins can create and edit dashboards. Read-only users can view them.

TypeShows Numeric tile The current value, large, with optional prefix and suffix. Sparkline A small trend line under the value. Line chart One or more signals over a time window. Gauge The value on a round scale with coloured thresholds. Bar indicator The value as a bar between min and max. Status A coloured state from thresholds, for example OK / warning / alarm. Named-value table Every NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT signal with Value, Age and Src. Filter accepts a substring or a *.glob. A widget shows Stale when no sample has arrived for 5 seconds, and No samples yet when the signal has never been seen.

MAVLink fields: every numeric field the flight controller sends (attitude, VFR HUD, battery, GPS, home, RTK, failsafe, heartbeat and status values) appears automatically, with friendly names and units where known. Named values: NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT signals, shown as NAME@sysid:compid, for example LTE_RSRP@1:194. You can type a signal that isn't sending yet and press Enter to add it, so you can build the board before you wire up the sensor. Use the pencil icon on a selected source to give it a display name.

UAVcast-Pro keeps a short history of every signal on the drone (up to 3600 samples per signal, about one hour at 1 Hz), so charts are filled as soon as you open a dashboard, even after a page refresh.

Export JSON copies the dashboard to the clipboard. Import JSON creates a dashboard from pasted JSON. Use it to copy a board to another drone. Duplicate and Rename are in the toolbar; Delete removes a dashboard and its widgets. Fullscreen hides the rest of the interface, for a dedicated monitor.

Pairing connects a drone running UAVcast-Pro to your organization in UAVmatrix Fleet Manager, the cloud dashboard for your fleet. Once paired, the drone keeps a certificate-authenticated, encrypted connection to Fleet Manager and reconnects by itself after a reboot or a network change. You start pairing on the drone and finish it in Fleet Manager. It takes about two minutes.

Connect a Pixhawk or any other ArduPilot or PX4 flight controller to UAVcast-Pro over USB or UART, with automatic port and baud detection and a live connection check. UAVcast-Pro reads MAVLink from your flight controller (ArduPilot, PX4 or any other MAVLink autopilot) over USB or a UART (TELEM port) and forwards it to every ground station you add. With Port and Baud rate on Automatic, the default, it finds the flight controller by itself, remembers what worked and reconnects after a reboot, USB glitch or late power-up. You'll find it under Flight Controller → Connection. <drone-ip>/flight-controller Flight Controller → Connection with a USB link to a Pixhawk.
k: UAVcast-Pro, UAVmatrix, Fleet Manager, drone 4G LTE, MAVLink, ArduPilot, PX4, QGroundControl, Mission Planner, Raspberry Pi drone video

c: Plug the flight controller's USB port into the companion computer with a data-capable cable. Go to Flight Controller → Connection and select USB under Link type. Leave Port on Automatic. USB connections don't use a baud rate. If the status panel says Link stopped, select Connect. Within a few seconds the status reads CONNECTED with the vehicle type and system ID, for example Connected to Quadrotor (system 1) on ArduPilot fmuv2 (ttyACM0).

Wire the TELEM port: flight controller TX → RX on the companion computer, RX → TX, and GND → GND. Don't connect 5 V if both boards have their own supply. On the flight controller, set the port to MAVLink 2: for TELEM2 that's SERIAL2_PROTOCOL = 2. Note SERIAL2_BAUD. In UAVcast-Pro, select UART / Serial under Link type. Leave Port and Baud rate on Automatic, or pick the port (on a Raspberry Pi the GPIO UART is marked recommended) and the baud rate that matches SERIALx_BAUD. Select Connect if the link is stopped. Changes apply immediately. You don't need to restart anything. Automatic baud rate In automatic mode UAVcast-Pro tries 57600, 115200, 921600, 1500000, 460800, 230400 and 500000 baud, starting with the last rate that worked. If heartbeats stop for 20 seconds while data still arrives (for example after you change SERIALx_BAUD), it searches again.

SettingDefaultValuesNotes Link enabled On On, off Off releases the serial port and stops telemetry to all ground stations. Link type USB USB, UART / Serial Decides which ports Automatic searches. Port Automatic Automatic, a detected port, Custom path… Automatic prefers the stable /dev/serial/by-id/… path and follows the device if its number changes. Custom path takes any device such as /dev/ttyAMA0. Ports used by another program show in use by …. Baud rate Automatic Automatic or a fixed rate Ignored for USB. Must match SERIALx_BAUD when fixed.

StateMeaning Connected Heartbeats are arriving. Connected for, Last heartbeat and Auto-reconnects show the link's health. Waiting for device The port doesn't exist. The flight controller is unplugged, unpowered or still booting. Detecting baud rate Trying baud rates (Trying 115200 baud (2 of 7)). No heartbeat The port is open but no valid MAVLink arrives: wrong baud rate, TX/RX swapped, or the port isn't set to MAVLink. Reconnecting The link dropped and is coming back by itself. The Connection check card, updated every second, follows the data from the wire to the ground station. The first row that isn't green is the problem: Flight controller plugged in (USB) or Serial port available (UART). Not detected usually means a charge-only USB cable or no power. Signal on the wire: bytes arrive on the port. Readable flight controller data: bytes decode as MAVLink. % damaged points to a loose or long wire, a missing ground or noise from power cables. Flight controller responding: heartbeats from the vehicle. Sending to ground station: packets per second to each enabled destination, or No ground station set up.

Auto-detect pauses the link, listens on every serial port at every baud rate, saves the port and speed it finds and starts the link with them. Use it when you don't know which port or baud rate the flight controller uses. Show what was tried lists every attempt.

The right-hand column shows the live vehicle state: connection, GCS Failsafe Information, Vehicle Information (type, controller, flight mode, armed), Battery Status, GPS Information and flight data. If the panel shows Warning - Failsafe Disabled, the flight controller has no GCS failsafe. Enable it (FS_GCS_ENABLE on ArduPilot) before flying over a cellular link.

UAVcast-Pro doesn't accept incoming telemetry connections. The TCP server on port 5760 that mavlink-router normally opens is turned off, so only ground stations you add on Ground Control Stations get telemetry, and only while Enable Telemetry is on. Coming from an older version Earlier versions defaulted to /dev/ttyACM0 at 57600 baud and accepted TCP connections on port 5760. Since v6.4.3 every device moves to Automatic once, with the old port and baud tried first. Since v6.5.0, TCP 5760 is closed: add your PC as a ground station and connect over UDP instead.

Use UAVcast-Pro injectors to push sensor readings from scripts, Arduinos or the LTE modem into the MAVLink stream over HTTP, UDP or serial, so QGC and Mission Planner see them. An injector feeds data from outside UAVcast-Pro, such as a Python script, an Arduino or a sensor on the network, into the MAVLink stream as NAMED_VALUE_FLOAT (or NAMED_VALUE_INT) messages. Every connected ground station receives the values as normal telemetry: Mission Planner shows them in the Status tab and QGroundControl in the MAVLink Inspector. They also appear automatically in Data Streams dashboards. Open Flight Controller → Injectors. Typical uses: radiation, gas or weather sensors on the companion computer, LTE signal values (RSRP, SINR) for link monitoring, or values your own scripts compute.

Stream RTCM3 corrections from an NTRIP caster over 4G/LTE to your flight controller for RTK Fixed positioning. Caster, mountpoint, VRS and GGA settings. UAVcast-Pro has a built-in NTRIP client. It connects to an NTRIP v1 or v2 caster over the drone's internet link, receives RTCM3 corrections and passes them to the flight controller as MAVLink GPS_RTCM_DATA, the same way Mission Planner's "Inject GPS" does, but from the drone itself. Track your drone live on the UAVcast-Pro Flight Map with a cockpit HUD, video windows, arm/disarm, flight modes, RTL, loiter, GCS failsafe and flight controller messages. The Flight Map is a browser-based ground station built into UAVcast-Pro. It shows the drone on a map with its trail, the active mission and home position, a cockpit HUD, live video, and the flight controller's messages. You can arm and disarm, change flight mode, start a mission and trigger RTL or loiter, all behind confirmation dialogs. Open Flight Map → Map view. It's meant for monitoring and simple commands from any phone, tablet or laptop. For full mission planning and parameter work, keep using Mission Planner or QGroundControl alongside it. <drone-ip>/flight-map Flight Map → Map view on a bench unit without a GPS fix, so the map shows no drone position.

c: Map (left): the drone with heading, trail, home marker and mission. Sats shows the satellite count; Auto-Pan keeps the drone centred. Switch layers with the layer button (Street Map, Satellite and others). If the drone has no fix you see No GPS Lock: At least 4 satellites required. Top bar: the Recording buttons (Telemetry, CAM 1, CAM 2), free recording space, the telemetry update rate (1 Hz to 10 Hz), the current data rate, and a button that opens the map in its own window. Cockpit (right): an attitude HUD with speed and altitude tapes, the current flight mode, the arm state, battery voltage and the latest pre-arm message. Side tabs: Status, Gauge, Actions, Messages and Recordings. Drag the panel edge to resize it; double-click the handle to reset. Video windows: one per active camera stream. Drag, maximize, minimize or hide them; hidden windows dock as tabs at the bottom of the map. The top bar across every page also shows FC Connected, Armed/Disarmed, the vehicle type, the flight mode, and GCS Failsafe Enabled or GCS Failsafe Disabled.

Open the Actions tab, or use the arm control under the cockpit. Select Arm. The dialog warns The propellers can start spinning. Make sure nobody is near the drone and the area around it is clear. Confirm with Arm. The flight controller's own pre-arm checks still decide. If it refuses, you see The drone refused to arm. Check the PreArm message on the screen. The reason appears under the cockpit and in Messages. Disarm stops the motors immediately. The flight controller refuses it while the drone is flying.

Pick a mode from the flight mode control. The list matches the vehicle type (Copter, Plane, Rover, Sub) and is grouped into Safe Modes (position hold and stabilization), Navigation (autonomous modes) and Advanced (manual and emergency modes). Modes with a higher risk are marked with a warning icon and ask for confirmation before the command is sent.

Read-only users see the Actions tab but can't use it (Read-only users can't control the drone).

Messages lists every text message from the flight controller. Active alerts shows the current problems (for example pre-arm failures) separately from the Message log. Status: cards for LINK (packet loss, connected), FLIGHT CONTROLLER (armed, mode, vehicle), telemetry data rate, position, GPS (lock, satellites, ALTITUDE (AGL), ALTITUDE (AMSL)) and BATTERY. c: RSSI: the receiver's signal strength from the flight controller, rated No Signal, Weak, Fair, Good or Excellent. It needs RSSI to be set up on the flight controller (RSSI_TYPE on ArduPilot). Primary Controls: Channel 1 - Roll, Channel 2 - Pitch, Channel 3 - Throttle and Channel 4 - Yaw, in the Mission Planner layout. Auxiliary Channels: the remaining channels. PWM values typically range from 1000 (min) to 2000 (max). A channel that never moves means it isn't mapped on the transmitter, or the receiver doesn't send it. The values come from the flight controller's RC_CHANNELS message, so they only update while the flight controller link is Connected.

Add ground station destinations in UAVcast-Pro to stream MAVLink telemetry (UDP 14550) and H.264 video (UDP 5600) to Mission Planner, QGroundControl or several PCs. A destination tells UAVcast-Pro where to send telemetry and video. Each one is an IP address plus a telemetry port and a video port. UAVcast-Pro sends to every enabled destination at the same time over UDP, so Mission Planner on one laptop and QGroundControl on a tablet can both receive the drone. Open Ground Control Stations in the sidebar. <drone-ip>/ground-control Two destination cards: a disabled, empty one and an enabled destination with telemetry and video on.

Use the ports your ground station listens on. Turn on Enable Telemetry and, if you want video, Enable Video. Every field saves when you press Enter or leave it. There is no Save button. Telemetry routing picks up the change within a few seconds. Secure the UAVcast-Pro web interface with an admin login, add read-only users who can watch telemetry and video but not control the drone, and change or reset passwords. A fresh UAVcast-Pro install has no users and no login: anyone who can open the web interface has full admin rights. Add an admin user to turn on the login. After that, you can add Read Only users for observers, customers or payload operators who should see everything but change nothing. Open Management → Users. <drone-ip>/users Management → Users with the Add New User dialog open.
k: UAVcast-Pro, UAVmatrix, Fleet Manager, drone 4G LTE, MAVLink, ArduPilot, PX4, QGroundControl, Mission Planner, Raspberry Pi drone video

c: Go to Users and select Add User. Enter a Username (at least 3 characters), a Password (at least 6 characters) and Confirm Password. Select Create User. The first user is always an Admin (First user must be an admin). From now on every visitor gets a login page. A login lasts 7 days on that browser, or until you select Logout in the user menu at the bottom of the sidebar. The web interface uses plain HTTP Logins and settings travel unencrypted. That's fine on your own LAN or inside a VPN, but never forward the web interface's port to the internet.

Can…AdminRead Only See the Dashboard, Data Streams, Flight Controller, Flight Map, Ground Control Stations and Camera pages Yes Yes Watch live video and telemetry, view dashboards and recordings Yes Yes Change any setting Yes No Arm, disarm, change mode, start or clear missions Yes No Start or stop recordings Yes No Open Modem, Virtual Private Network, Dynamic DNS, Networks, Fleet Management, Users and Application Yes No (hidden) You can't create a Read Only user before an admin exists (Create an admin user first before adding read-only users). Read-only web users are different from the Read Only switch on a ground station destination, which blocks commands from a ground station program. See Ground control stations.
Select Change Password, enter the Current Password and the New Password twice, and select Update Password. Passwords are stored as bcrypt hashes.

Select Delete on the user's row and confirm. You can't delete your own account while other users exist. Deleting the last user turns the login off again: After deletion, the application will be open without authentication until a new user is created.

There's no reset link, because the drone has no email, and password recovery isn't self-service. If another admin can still log in, they can delete your user under Users and create it again. If nobody with the admin role can log in, contact support at support@uavmatrix.com. Include your license key (or the email you bought it with), the device's hostname or name as shown under Application → License Manager → Activated Devices, the UAVcast-Pro version, and whether you can reach the device over SSH.
